claims: Flying sprints use a progressive run-in to reach high velocity before a short maximal-velocity zone.
{{canonicalName}} must separate run-in distance, measured fly-zone distance, intent, and timing method from its stable exercise identity.
Acceleration, maximal velocity, and speed endurance are related but distinct sprint-training qualities.
{{canonicalName}} belongs to upright high-speed locomotion; dense repeated-sprint conditioning requires a separate delivery profile.
Maximal-velocity exposures impose meaningful eccentric hamstring demand in addition to whole-lower-limb and trunk demands.
The card should identify bilateral hip, knee, and ankle actions, posterior-chain loading, calf-foot stiffness demand, and trunk-pelvis control.
Maximal running velocity depends on the interaction of step length, step rate, short contact time, force production, and coordinated upright sprint mechanics.
Coaching should preserve individual solutions and avoid forcing one universal limb position or artificially reaching for stride length.
Unresisted flying, resisted, assisted, and combined sprint methods create materially different kinematic and force-velocity demands.
Exercise difficulty must score physical demand and technical complexity directly, including coordination, supervision, impact, and failure consequence; it must not use a skill-library level.
Weekly high-speed sprint exposure can measurably affect eccentric hamstring force capacity.
{{canonicalName}} needs explicit high-speed distance, contact, neural-intent, posterior-chain stress, performance-drop, session-recovery, and weekly-exposure tracking.
Flying and wicket drills require a suitable running surface, marked zones, progressive build-in, and a clear deceleration area.
Footwear, weather, lane separation, equipment placement, timing setup, run-out distance, and coach sightline are hard delivery constraints.
Run-in and fly-zone length should match the athlete's ability to reach and briefly preserve maximal velocity.
Prescribe build-in distance, fly-zone distance, total high-speed distance, repetitions, intensity, inter-repetition recovery, and a performance-drop stop rule.
The athlete should accelerate progressively into upright high-speed mechanics rather than attack the fly zone from a cold or abrupt start.
Use a small number of observable cues: build smoothly, run tall without leaning back, strike beneath the body, keep arm action coordinated, sprint through the zone, and decelerate gradually.
High-speed sprint load and recent exposure must be monitored rather than inferred from repetition count alone.
Stop for pain, hamstring or calf tightness, limping, stumble, unsafe surface or spacing, repeated overstriding, loss of upright control, or a persistent velocity or timing decline.
Flying sprints are used to develop maximal velocity and should continue only while velocity and mechanics remain stable.
{{canonicalName}} belongs early in a session after preparation and before fatigue-oriented work; rehabilitation, conditioning, and assisted-speed uses require separate contextual profiles.
Fly-in work isolates a short maximal-velocity action zone after an acceleration zone.
Athlete-facing support should show the zone layout, define a successful rep, limit the cue count, state the run-out expectation, and explain the stop signal.
Coaches can use marked fly zones and timing to observe or monitor top-speed performance.
Coach support should include setup measurements, athlete-specific build-in choice, contact and posture observations, split consistency, spacing control, regression choices, and recovery decisions.
Speed work should be developmentally appropriate and follow movement competency, readiness, and progressive exposure.
Intent, run-in length, fly-zone length, timing pressure, cue complexity, wicket spacing, and total exposure can be scaled without assigning the exercise a skill level.
Normal, resisted, assisted, and combined sprinting produce different training conditions and should not be collapsed into one undifferentiated card.
Fly-zone length is dosage, run-in style is usually a variant, and external assistance or resistance may require a distinct definition when it changes the primary stimulus and safety model.

assessmentSummary.identity: A progressive run-in followed by a short 10-yard or 10-meter maximal-velocity zone and a controlled run-out.
currentCardFindings: The current description captures a build-in and run-out but the controlled taxonomy, anatomy, constraints, load, and fatigue fields are empty.
Uniform low difficulty values understate the technical coordination, impact, supervision, posterior-chain load, and consequence of error at maximal velocity.
Flying 10 and Flying 10m Sprint appear to be the same identity with unit and wording differences rather than separate exercises.
assessmentSummary.programmingDecision: Retain one Flying 10 identity. Store yards versus meters, run-in distance, timing method, and target intensity as dosage or delivery metadata. Program fresh with full recovery and stop when mechanics or time deteriorate.

assessmentSummary.identity: A three-zone progressive run in which the athlete builds speed, increases speed, then runs fast but relaxed across equal 20-unit segments.
currentCardFindings: The description defines the three zones but controlled taxonomy, anatomy, constraints, load, and fatigue fields are empty.
Its physical demand is understated because the 60-unit total exposure and final high-speed segment create greater work-capacity and recovery demands than a short Flying 10.
Yards versus meters and small segment-length changes belong in dosage rather than new identities.
assessmentSummary.programmingDecision: Retain as a progressive three-zone build-up profile. Define whether the final zone is submaximal rhythm work or maximal-velocity exposure, prescribe all zone lengths and target intent, and keep a separate conditioning profile if recovery is shortened.

assessmentSummary.identity: An upright sprint through athlete-spaced mini-hurdle wickets that constrain step rhythm and contact location during a max-velocity-oriented run.
currentCardFindings: The card names front-side cycle, elastic contact, and upright posture but does not define wicket height, number, individualized spacing, run-in, run-out, or progression rules.
Controlled equipment, environment, anatomy, load, fatigue, and complete difficulty fields are empty.
Uniform 40 difficulty values substantially understate spacing judgment, coordination, equipment setup, supervision, and error consequences.
assessmentSummary.programmingDecision: Retain a wicket-run definition because the environmental constraint and equipment materially change execution and coaching. Require individualized spacing, a progressive run-in, clear run-out, low wicket height, and immediate regression when the athlete reaches, chops, clips wickets, or loses rhythm.

claims: Mini-hurdle wickets provide external spacing cues intended to support upright posture, front-side action, and powerful knee lift.
Spacing should respond to athlete speed and stature; wickets must not be used to force reaching or an artificial universal stride length.
Wicket runs require measured mini-hurdle placement on a safe track or turf surface.
The card needs wicket height, count, athlete-specific spacing, build-in, lane width, run-out, footwear, collision control, and coach placement.
Wicket-run volume should be prescribed as quality repetitions with complete zone and equipment setup rather than as an unspecified drill count.
Progress spacing only when the athlete clears the wickets without reaching, chopping, clipping, or losing upright rhythm.
